items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a vertical grid line on a map, numbered from west to east and read first in a grid reference”.
items.answer: Easting
items.markingKey: Easting: a vertical grid line on a map, numbered from west to east and read first in a grid reference. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a six-figure grid reference is more useful than a four-figure reference for locating a building.
items.answer: A four-figure reference only identifies a 1 km grid square; a six-figure reference divides the square into tenths in each direction, locating a point to within 100 m.
items.markingKey: 1 mark four-figure = whole square; 1 mark six-figure = point within 100 m [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the straight-line distance and the distance by road between two places.
items.answer: Straight-line distance is the shortest direct distance; roads bend around relief, rivers and buildings, so the road distance is longer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: On Fig. 4.1, a map of part of a rural area, the campsite lies in the grid square whose south-west corner is where easting 66 meets northing 55. The symbol is 3 tenths of the way across the square (eastwards) and 7 tenths of the way up (northwards). Give (a) the four-figure and (b) the six-figure grid reference of the campsite.
items.markingKey: (a) 6655 [1] (b) 663557: easting first, then northing [1]

items.stem: On Fig. 1.1 (part of a 1:25 000 topographic map), the trig point lies in the grid square whose south-west corner is where easting 59 meets northing 55. The symbol is 7 tenths of the way across the square (eastwards) and 3 tenths of the way up (northwards). A lighthouse is at 613574. The grid lines are 1 km apart. (a) Give the six-figure grid reference of the trig point. (b) Suggest why a walker might travel further than this to get from the trig point to the lighthouse.
items.answer: (a) 597553 (b) Paths and roads bend around steep slopes, rivers, woodland and private land, so the route is longer than a straight line.
items.markingKey: (a) 597553 (eastings first) [1] (b) 1 mark obstacle/relief; 1 mark route not straight [2]

items.stem: On the topographic map extract (scale 1:50 000), the farm lies in the grid square whose south-west corner is where easting 59 meets northing 33. The symbol is 3 tenths of the way across the square (eastwards) and 4 tenths of the way up (northwards). A campsite is at 619355. The grid lines are 1 km apart. (a) Give the six-figure grid reference of the farm. (b) State the compass direction (eight points) of the campsite from the farm. (c) Suggest why a walker might travel further than this to get from the farm to the campsite.
items.answer: (a) 593334 (b) North-east (c) Paths and roads bend around steep slopes, rivers, woodland and private land, so the route is longer than a straight line.
items.markingKey: (a) 593334 (eastings first) [1] (b) Bearing about 051°, so north-east [1] (c) 1 mark obstacle/relief; 1 mark route not straight [2]

items.stem: “Paper topographic maps are no longer needed now that people use digital mapping and satellite navigation.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: remote areas; cost; interpreting relief.
items.answer: For: Digital maps update quickly, zoom in and out and show live information such as traffic. GPS gives an exact location without needing grid references. Against: Phones lose signal and battery in remote areas, so walkers and rescue teams still carry paper maps. Contours, symbols and scale are the same skills needed to read digital maps. Paper maps show a wide area at once for planning. Judgement: Digital tools have changed map use, but map skills and paper maps are still needed, especially in remote areas and emergencies.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that paper topographic maps are no longer needed now that people use digital mapping and satellite navigation. You may wish to consider: reliability; cost.
items.answer: For: Digital maps update quickly, zoom in and out and show live information such as traffic. GPS gives an exact location without needing grid references. Paper maps show a wide area at once for planning. Judgement: Digital tools have changed map use, but map skills and paper maps are still needed, especially in remote areas and emergencies.

items.stem: A student writes: “In a grid reference you read the northing before the easting.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Eastings are always given first (along the corridor, then up the stairs).
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is important to check the scale before measuring distances on a map.
items.answer: The same map distance represents very different ground distances at different scales (e.g. 1 cm = 250 m at 1:25 000 but 500 m at 1:50 000).
items.markingKey: 1 mark scale varies; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map, a footpath from the radio mast to the lighthouse measures 7 cm. Calculate the length of the footpath on the ground in kilometres. Show your working.
items.answer: 3.5 km

items.stem: A walking group plans a route on a 1:10 000 map. The route from the church with a tower to the windmill measures 4 cm. (a) Calculate the real distance in km. (b) The group walks at 5 km/h. Calculate the walking time in minutes on flat ground. (c) The route climbs 120 m. Using the rule of adding 1 minute for every 10 m of ascent, calculate the total time.
items.answer: (a) 0.4 km (b) 4.8 minutes (c) 16.8 minutes

items.stem: Evaluate the view that paper topographic maps are no longer needed now that people use digital mapping and satellite navigation.
items.answer: For: Digital maps update quickly, zoom in and out and show live information such as traffic. GPS gives an exact location without needing grid references. Against: Phones lose signal and battery in remote areas, so walkers and rescue teams still carry paper maps. Contours, symbols and scale are the same skills needed to read digital maps. Paper maps show a wide area at once for planning. Judgement: Digital tools have changed map use, but map skills and paper maps are still needed, especially in remote areas and emergencies.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a line on a map joining places of equal height above sea level”.
items.answer: Contour line
items.markingKey: Contour line: a line on a map joining places of equal height above sea level. [1]

items.stem: Explain how you can tell from contour lines whether a slope is concave or convex.
items.answer: Concave: contours close together at the top and wider apart lower down. Convex: contours wide apart at the top and close together lower down.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Describe how to draw a cross-section between two points on a map.
items.answer: Place the straight edge of paper between the points; mark and label each contour it crosses; transfer the marks to the horizontal axis of graph paper; plot each height and join with a smooth line; label features and add scales.
items.markingKey: 1 mark marking contours; 1 mark plotting heights; 1 mark smooth line/labels [3]

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 describes part of a topographic map. A river flows west in a wide valley at about 40 m. To the east the land rises: contours are widely spaced up to 120 m, then crowded together up to a summit marked by a spot height of 186 m. A small stream valley cuts into the slope, shown by contours forming Vs pointing east. State whether the slope east of the river is concave or convex. Give a reason.
items.answer: Convex: contours are wide apart lower down and close together near the top.
items.markingKey: 1 mark convex; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.2, which describes a map extract. Contours at a 10 m interval run from 40 m beside a river in the west to 180 m at a summit in the east. In the west they are wide apart; east of the 120 m contour they are very close together. A spot height of 186 m marks the summit. V-shaped contours point east along a stream that flows west. (a) State the height of the summit. (b) Explain which direction the small stream flows and how you know.
items.answer: (a) 186 m (spot height). (b) West, downhill towards the river: the contour Vs point upstream (east), towards higher land.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark west; 1 mark V points uphill/upstream [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.2, which describes a map extract. Contours at a 10 m interval run from 40 m beside a river in the west to 180 m at a summit in the east. In the west they are wide apart; east of the 120 m contour they are very close together. A spot height of 186 m marks the summit. V-shaped contours point east along a stream that flows west. (a) State whether the slope east of the river is concave or convex. Give a reason. (b) Suggest why settlement is more likely in the west of the area.
items.answer: (a) Convex: contours are wide apart lower down and close together near the top. (b) Flat, low land near the river is easier to build on and farm, with water supply and easier routes; the steep east is hard to build on.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark convex; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark flat land; 1 mark water/access [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the difference in height between two neighbouring contour lines”.
items.answer: Contour interval
items.markingKey: Contour interval: the difference in height between two neighbouring contour lines. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “If contour lines are far apart, the land must be very high.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Spacing shows steepness, not height; widely spaced contours show a gentle slope at any height. The contour values show height.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map with a contour interval of 5 m, the farm lies on the 40 m contour and the car park lies on the 65 m contour. They are 4 cm apart on the map. (a) Calculate the difference in height. (b) Calculate the horizontal distance between them in metres. (c) State how many contour lines you cross walking between them, not counting the one you start on.
Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values”.
items.answer: Mean
items.markingKey: Mean: the average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the median is sometimes a better average than the mean.
items.answer: The median is not affected by extreme values (anomalies), so it better represents a typical value when data are uneven.
items.markingKey: 1 mark median = middle value; 1 mark not distorted by extremes [2]

items.stem: Explain why a strong correlation on a scatter graph does not prove that one variable causes the other.
items.answer: Both may be linked to a third factor, or the link may be coincidence; correlation only shows that they change together.
items.markingKey: 1 mark third factor/coincidence; 1 mark correlation ≠ causation [2]

items.stem: The table shows pebble length (mm) sampled along a beach near Lisbon: sample 1 82, sample 2 43, sample 3 84, sample 4 14, sample 5 34. Identify the sample with the highest value and state by how much it exceeds the mean.
items.answer: sample 3, 32.6 mm above the mean

items.stem: The table shows river velocity (m/s) at sites downstream along a river near Kuala Lumpur: site 1 1.33, site 2 0.26, site 3 0.88, site 4 0.97, site 5 0.99, site 6 0.61, site 7 0.76, site 8 0.9, site 9 1.04. (a) Find the median. (b) Identify the site with the highest value and state by how much it exceeds the mean.
items.answer: (a) 0.9 m/s (b) site 1, 0.47 m/s above the mean

items.stem: The table shows pebble length (mm) sampled along a beach near Cape Town: sample 1 82, sample 2 32, sample 3 19, sample 4 80, sample 5 30, sample 6 79, sample 7 39, sample 8 84, sample 9 59. (a) Identify the sample with the highest value and state by how much it exceeds the mean. (b) Suggest one way of presenting these data and give a reason.
items.answer: (a) sample 8, 28 mm above the mean (b) A bar graph, because the data are separate (discrete) categories that can be compared by bar height.
items.markingKey: (a) 84 − 56 = 28 [2] (b) 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: “A single type of graph is enough to present the results of a geographical investigation.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: A simple bar or line graph may clearly show the main pattern. Against: Different data need different techniques: scatter graphs for relationships, pie charts for proportions, maps for spatial patterns. Combining graphs and maps (e.g. located bar graphs) shows both pattern and location. Judgement: Usually not: the best investigations choose a range of techniques suited to each type of data.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that a single type of graph is enough to present the results of a geographical investigation? Use examples you have studied. You may wish to consider: spatial patterns; type of data; relationships.
items.answer: For: A simple bar or line graph may clearly show the main pattern. Against: Different data need different techniques: scatter graphs for relationships, pie charts for proportions, maps for spatial patterns. Combining graphs and maps (e.g. located bar graphs) shows both pattern and location. Judgement: Usually not: the best investigations choose a range of techniques suited to each type of data.

Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: A student writes: “The range tells you the average value of a data set.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The range measures spread (highest minus lowest), not the average.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain what you should include when describing the trend shown by a line graph.
items.answer: The overall direction (increase/decrease), changes in rate, the highest and lowest points and any anomalies, with figures and dates quoted from the graph.
items.markingKey: 1 mark trend; 1 mark use of data/units [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.3 is a line graph showing the annual rainfall at Kuala Lumpur (mm). The values plotted are: 2017: 585, 2018: 581, 2019: 548, 2020: 706, 2021: 848, 2022: 1072, 2023: 1319. (a) Calculate the percentage change between 2017 and 2023. (b) Suggest why a line graph is suitable for these data.
items.answer: (a) +125.5% (b) The data are continuous over time, so a line shows the trend and rate of change between dates.

items.stem: Fig. 1.3 is a line graph showing the annual rainfall at Lima (mm). The values plotted are: 2017: 647, 2018: 705, 2019: 751, 2020: 998, 2021: 1094, 2022: 970, 2023: 1281. (a) Describe the trend shown by Fig. 1.3. Use data in your answer. (b) Identify the period with the greatest increase. (c) Suggest why a line graph is suitable for these data.
items.answer: (a) Overall an increase from 647 mm (2017) to 1281 mm (2023), with fluctuations; highest 1281 mm in 2023, lowest 647 mm in 2017. (b) 2022-2023 (+311 mm) (c) The data are continuous over time, so a line shows the trend and rate of change between dates.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark overall trend; 1 mark change in rate/fluctuation; 1 mark data with units [3] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a detailed label on a sketch, map or photograph that explains or describes a feature”.
items.answer: Annotation
items.markingKey: Annotation: a detailed label on a sketch, map or photograph that explains or describes a feature. [1]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a short name added to a diagram to identify a feature”.
items.answer: Label
items.markingKey: Label: a short name added to a diagram to identify a feature. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a field sketch can be more useful than a photograph.
items.answer: It selects and simplifies the important features, which can be annotated to explain processes; photographs include irrelevant detail.
items.markingKey: 1 mark selection/simplification; 1 mark annotations explain [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.5 is a photograph of a coastline. In the foreground is a wide, rocky wave-cut platform exposed at low tide. In the middle distance a steep chalk cliff about 30 m high has a cave at its base and a narrow arch at the headland. In the background two isolated pillars of rock stand in the sea. Grass covers the cliff top, with a footpath close to the edge. Describe the cliff shown in Fig. 1.5.
items.answer: Steep (vertical) chalk cliff about 30 m high, with a cave at its base; grass on top.
items.markingKey: 1 mark steep; 1 mark height/rock/feature [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.6, two satellite images of a rainforest area. The 2005 image shows continuous forest crossed by a single new road. By 2025, side roads branch off the main road and land on both sides has been cleared for pasture and crops, leaving about 60% of the forest. (a) Explain one advantage of satellite images for monitoring deforestation. (b) Suggest two impacts of the changes shown on the local environment.
items.answer: (a) They cover large, remote areas regularly so the rate and location of clearing can be measured and illegal clearing detected. (b) Loss of habitat and biodiversity; soil erosion and nutrient loss; less evapotranspiration, so less rainfall; more CO₂ released.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark coverage/repeat; 1 mark use [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.6 is a pair of satellite images of the same area of tropical forest, taken in 2005 and 2025. In 2005 almost all the area is dark green forest with one road running east-west. In 2025 a “fishbone” pattern of light-coloured cleared strips runs north and south from the road; about 40% of the area is cleared, with small settlements and cattle pasture. Suggest why the clearing is concentrated near roads.
items.answer: Roads give access for machinery and settlers and allow cattle, timber and crops to be transported to market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark access; 1 mark transport to market [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a horizontal grid line on a map, numbered from south to north and read second in a grid reference”.
items.answer: Northing
items.markingKey: Northing: a horizontal grid line on a map, numbered from south to north and read second in a grid reference. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A 1:25 000 map shows more detail than a 1:50 000 map of the same area.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It is a larger scale: 1 cm represents 250 m instead of 500 m, so features are shown larger and in more detail.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe how to give a compass bearing from point A to point B on a map.
items.answer: Draw a line from A to B; place a protractor on A with 0° pointing to grid north; measure the angle clockwise from north to the line; write it as three figures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark line and north; 1 mark clockwise; 1 mark three figures [3]

items.stem: On a map, the windmill is 4 km south of the quarry. (a) State the compass direction of the windmill from the quarry. (b) Give the three-figure bearing. (c) State the bearing you would follow to return from the windmill to the quarry.
items.answer: (a) South (b) 180° (c) 000° (north)
items.markingKey: (a) south [1] (b) 180° clockwise from north [1] (c) 000°: add or subtract 180° [1]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map (2 cm grid squares, each 1 km²), an area of farmland completely covers 15 grid squares and covers about 0.25 of each of 2 other squares. Explain why counting squares gives only an estimate of area.
items.answer: Part-squares must be judged by eye, and the edge of the feature is irregular, so the total is approximate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark partial squares; 1 mark irregular boundary [2]

items.stem: Nadia argues that paper topographic maps are no longer needed now that people use digital mapping and satellite navigation. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: remote areas; cost.
items.answer: For: Digital maps update quickly, zoom in and out and show live information such as traffic. GPS gives an exact location without needing grid references. Against: Phones lose signal and battery in remote areas, so walkers and rescue teams still carry paper maps. Contours, symbols and scale are the same skills needed to read digital maps. Paper maps show a wide area at once for planning. Judgement: Digital tools have changed map use, but map skills and paper maps are still needed, especially in remote areas and emergencies.

Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a dot on a map with a number showing the exact height of that point in metres”.
items.answer: Spot height
items.markingKey: Spot height: a dot on a map with a number showing the exact height of that point in metres. [1]

items.stem: Explain how to tell a spur from a valley on a contour map.
items.answer: In a valley the V-shaped contours point uphill (and a river often flows along it); on a spur the Vs point downhill towards lower land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark valley; 1 mark spur [2]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map with a contour interval of 10 m, the railway station lies on the 200 m contour and the museum lies on the 300 m contour. They are 2.5 cm apart on the map. Calculate the average gradient, giving your answer as a ratio 1 : n.
items.markingKey: gradient = vertical ÷ horizontal = 100 : 1250 = 1 : 12.5 [2]

items.stem: “Relief is the most important factor affecting how land is used in an area.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Steep slopes limit building, roads and machinery; flat valley floors attract settlement, farming and routes. Height affects temperature and so crops. Against: Soil, drainage and climate also matter. Human factors such as markets, transport, planning laws and technology (terracing, tunnels) can overcome relief. Judgement: Relief strongly influences land use, but human factors and technology can modify its effect.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.2, which describes a map extract. Contours at a 10 m interval run from 40 m beside a river in the west to 180 m at a summit in the east. In the west they are wide apart; east of the 120 m contour they are very close together. A spot height of 186 m marks the summit. V-shaped contours point east along a stream that flows west. (a) State the height of the summit. (b) Describe the relief of the area shown. (c) Suggest why settlement is more likely in the west of the area.
items.answer: (a) 186 m (spot height). (b) Low, fairly flat land (about 40 m) by the river in the west; land rises gently to about 120 m, then steeply to a summit of 186 m in the east; the slope is cut by a small stream valley. (c) Flat, low land near the river is easier to build on and farm, with water supply and easier routes; the steep east is hard to build on.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark low west; 1 mark gentle then steep; 1 mark figures quoted [3] (c) 1 mark flat land; 1 mark water/access [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “mean”?
options: The average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values.
The middle value when all the values are placed in rank order.
The value that occurs most often in a set of data.
The difference between the highest and the lowest values in a data set.
items.answer: The average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values.
items.markingKey: Mean: the average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values. [1]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a choropleth map.
items.answer: Advantage: shows the spatial pattern clearly at a glance. Disadvantage: suggests the value is the same across each whole area and hides variation within areas; sudden changes at boundaries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why the range alone is not a good measure of the spread of data.
items.answer: It uses only the two extreme values, so one anomaly can make the range very large and it ignores how the other values are distributed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark uses extremes only; 1 mark affected by anomalies [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.3 is a line graph showing the area of mangrove forest along a coast near Lagos (km²). The values plotted are: 1990: 471, 1995: 540, 2000: 483, 2005: 584, 2010: 647, 2015: 848, 2020: 1141. (a) Identify the period with the greatest increase. (b) Suggest why a line graph is suitable for these data.
items.answer: (a) 2015-2020 (+293 km²) (b) The data are continuous over time, so a line shows the trend and rate of change between dates.

items.stem: A student surveys the ways students travel to a school in Karachi. Results (%): walk 60%, bus 30%, car 10%. (a) Identify the largest category and state its share as a fraction in its simplest form. (b) Suggest one other way of presenting these data and give one advantage of it.
items.answer: (a) walk: 3/5 (b) A divided (compound) bar graph: it is easy to draw accurately and several surveys can be compared side by side.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark category; 1 mark fraction [2] (b) 1 mark method; 1 mark advantage [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.4 is a scatter graph of channel width (m) against distance downstream (km) for 8 places. Points (x, y): (9, 47), (10, 25), (12, 56), (14, 66), (15, 67), (19, 74), (20, 81), (22, 84). (a) Describe the relationship shown by Fig. 1.4. (b) Identify the anomaly and explain why it is an anomaly. (c) Explain how a line of best fit should be drawn on Fig. 1.4.
items.answer: (a) A positive correlation: as distance downstream increases, channel width increases. (b) (10, 25): it lies far from the line of best fit and does not follow the positive trend. (c) A straight line through the middle of the points with roughly equal numbers above and below, ignoring the anomaly; it need not pass through the origin.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark type of correlation; 1 mark description with data [2] (b) 1 mark correct point; 1 mark reason [2] (c) 1 mark through the middle; 1 mark ignore anomaly [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Annotations on a sketch should only name the features shown.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. That is labelling; annotations add description or explanation, e.g. “wave-cut notch formed by hydraulic action”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.5, a photograph of a chalk headland. A rocky platform lies in front of a vertical cliff (about 30 m high) with a large cave at the bottom. At the end of the headland is an arch, and beyond it two stacks stand in the sea. A coastal path runs along the grassy cliff top. Suggest one hazard for people using the footpath and explain it.
items.answer: The path is close to the cliff edge; erosion and rock falls make the edge unstable, so people could fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hazard; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.6 is a pair of satellite images of the same area of tropical forest, taken in 2005 and 2025. In 2005 almost all the area is dark green forest with one road running east-west. In 2025 a “fishbone” pattern of light-coloured cleared strips runs north and south from the road; about 40% of the area is cleared, with small settlements and cattle pasture. (a) Explain one advantage of satellite images for monitoring deforestation. (b) Suggest two impacts of the changes shown on the local environment.
items.answer: (a) They cover large, remote areas regularly so the rate and location of clearing can be measured and illegal clearing detected. (b) Loss of habitat and biodiversity; soil erosion and nutrient loss; less evapotranspiration, so less rainfall; more CO₂ released.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark coverage/repeat; 1 mark use [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a map scale written as a ratio, such as 1:50 000, meaning one unit on the map is 50 000 of the same units on the ground”.
items.answer: Representative fraction
items.markingKey: Representative fraction: a map scale written as a ratio, such as 1:50 000, meaning one unit on the map is 50 000 of the same units on the ground. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “A bearing of 090° means travelling west.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so 090° is east and 270° is west.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the difference between the straight-line distance and the distance by road between two places. (b) A revision website states: “A bearing of 090° means travelling west.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Straight-line distance is the shortest direct distance; roads bend around relief, rivers and buildings, so the road distance is longer. (b) Not correct. Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so 090° is east and 270° is west.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: On a map, the farm is 1 km east and 1 km north of the quarry. (a) State the compass direction of the farm from the quarry. (b) Give the three-figure bearing. (c) State the bearing you would follow to return from the farm to the quarry.
items.answer: (a) North-east (b) 045° (c) 225° (south-west)
items.markingKey: (a) north-east [1] (b) 045° clockwise from north [1] (c) 225°: add or subtract 180° [1]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map (2 cm grid squares, each 1 km²), a nature reserve completely covers 8 grid squares and covers about 0.5 of each of 2 other squares. Estimate the area of a nature reserve in km².
items.answer: 9 km²

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that paper topographic maps are no longer needed now that people use digital mapping and satellite navigation? Use examples you have studied. You may wish to consider: remote areas; interpreting relief; reliability.
items.answer: For: Digital maps update quickly, zoom in and out and show live information such as traffic. GPS gives an exact location without needing grid references. Against: Phones lose signal and battery in remote areas, so walkers and rescue teams still carry paper maps. Contours, symbols and scale are the same skills needed to read digital maps. Paper maps show a wide area at once for planning. Judgement: Digital tools have changed map use, but map skills and paper maps are still needed, especially in remote areas and emergencies.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the steepness of a slope, found by dividing the vertical difference in height by the horizontal distance”.
items.answer: Gradient
items.markingKey: Gradient: the steepness of a slope, found by dividing the vertical difference in height by the horizontal distance. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the vertical scale of a cross-section is often exaggerated.
items.answer: Height differences are small compared with horizontal distances; exaggerating the vertical scale makes slopes and relief features visible.
items.markingKey: 1 mark small vertical change; 1 mark makes relief clear [2]

items.stem: A student draws a cross-section from X to Y. Heights read from the map every 250 m along the line are: 0 m from X, 100 m; 250 m from X, 100 m; 500 m from X, 140 m; 750 m from X, 120 m; 1000 m from X, 100 m; 1250 m from X, 80 m; 1500 m from X, 20 m. State the height and the distance from X of the highest point on the section.
items.answer: 140 m at 500 m from X
items.markingKey: 1 mark height; 1 mark distance [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 describes part of a topographic map. A river flows west in a wide valley at about 40 m. To the east the land rises: contours are widely spaced up to 120 m, then crowded together up to a summit marked by a spot height of 186 m. A small stream valley cuts into the slope, shown by contours forming Vs pointing east. (a) State the height of the summit. (b) State whether the slope east of the river is concave or convex. Give a reason. (c) Explain which direction the small stream flows and how you know. (d) Suggest why settlement is more likely in the west of the area.
items.answer: (a) 186 m (spot height). (b) Convex: contours are wide apart lower down and close together near the top. (c) West, downhill towards the river: the contour Vs point upstream (east), towards higher land. (d) Flat, low land near the river is easier to build on and farm, with water supply and easier routes; the steep east is hard to build on.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark convex; 1 mark reason [2] (c) 1 mark west; 1 mark V points uphill/upstream [2] (d) 1 mark flat land; 1 mark water/access [2]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map with a contour interval of 10 m, the car park lies on the 240 m contour and the lighthouse lies on the 280 m contour. They are 6 cm apart on the map. (a) Calculate the difference in height. (b) Calculate the horizontal distance between them in metres. (c) Calculate the average gradient, giving your answer as a ratio 1 : n. (d) State how many contour lines you cross walking between them, not counting the one you start on. (e) Suggest one reason why a cyclist would find this route difficult or easy.
items.answer: (a) 40 m (b) 3000 m (c) 1 : 75 (d) 4 (e) Fairly easy: 1 : 75 is a gentle gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) 280 − 240 = 40 m [1] (b) 6 cm × 50000 ÷ 100 = 3000 m [1] (c) gradient = vertical ÷ horizontal = 40 : 3000 = 1 : 75 [2] (d) 40 ÷ 10 = 4 [1] (e) 1 mark judgement linked to gradient value [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “median”?
options: A result that does not fit the general pattern or trend of the data.
The middle value when all the values are placed in rank order.
The difference between the highest and the lowest values in a data set.
The value that occurs most often in a set of data.
items.answer: The middle value when all the values are placed in rank order.
items.markingKey: Median: the middle value when all the values are placed in rank order. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A pie chart is the best way to show how rainfall changes through a year.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Change over time is best shown with a bar or line graph; pie charts show parts of a whole.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “If points on a scatter graph slope down from left to right, there is a negative correlation.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A classmate claims: “When describing a graph, you should quote figures with units.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. As one variable increases the other decreases. (b) Correct. Using data with units gives precise evidence and gains credit in 0460 mark schemes.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A student surveys the ways students travel to a school in Kathmandu. Results (%): walk 10%, bus 25%, car 30%, bicycle 35%. Calculate the angle of each sector for a pie chart.
items.answer: walk 36°, bus 90°, car 108°, bicycle 126°
items.markingKey: % × 3.6 for each; total 360° [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.4 is a scatter graph of pebble size (mm) against distance from the sea (km) for 8 places. Points (x, y): (1, 31), (2, 31), (8, 45), (9, 43), (11, 29), (15, 59), (23, 76), (28, 92). (a) Describe the relationship shown by Fig. 1.4. (b) Identify the anomaly and explain why it is an anomaly.
items.answer: (a) A positive correlation: as distance from the sea increases, pebble size increases. (b) (11, 29): it lies far from the line of best fit and does not follow the positive trend.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark type of correlation; 1 mark description with data [2] (b) 1 mark correct point; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: The table shows river velocity (m/s) at sites downstream along a river near Bogotá: site 1 1.17, site 2 1.13, site 3 0.49, site 4 0.65, site 5 1.21, site 6 1.39, site 7 0.84, site 8 1.3, site 9 1.26. (a) Find the median. (b) Calculate the range. (c) Identify the site with the highest value and state by how much it exceeds the mean. (d) Suggest one way of presenting these data and give a reason.
items.answer: (a) 1.17 m/s (b) 0.9 m/s (c) site 6, 0.34 m/s above the mean (d) A bar graph, because the data are separate (discrete) categories that can be compared by bar height.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A satellite image can show the extent of a flood that would be hard to see from the ground.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It covers a wide area at once, showing which land is under water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.6, two satellite images of a rainforest area. The 2005 image shows continuous forest crossed by a single new road. By 2025, side roads branch off the main road and land on both sides has been cleared for pasture and crops, leaving about 60% of the forest. Suggest why the clearing is concentrated near roads.
items.answer: Roads give access for machinery and settlers and allow cattle, timber and crops to be transported to market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark access; 1 mark transport to market [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.5, a photograph of a chalk headland. A rocky platform lies in front of a vertical cliff (about 30 m high) with a large cave at the bottom. At the end of the headland is an arch, and beyond it two stacks stand in the sea. A coastal path runs along the grassy cliff top. (a) Identify two landforms of erosion shown in Fig. 1.5. (b) Suggest one hazard for people using the footpath and explain it.
items.answer: (a) Any two: cliff, wave-cut platform, cave, arch, stack. (b) The path is close to the cliff edge; erosion and rock falls make the edge unstable, so people could fall.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark hazard; 1 mark explanation [2]
